MANILA, Philippines — The Bureau of Customs (BOC) is seeking to impose a mandatory deposit of at least P2 million in an escrow account of cargo deconsolidators alongside hefty fines for delivery failures, in order to safeguard balikbayan boxes sent home by overseas Filipino workers (OFWs).
Under the draft customs administrative order, deconsolidators accredited with other government agencies and who wish to conduct business with the agency shall apply for registration.
To guarantee compliance, the deconsolidator and agency should open an escrow account with a BOC-nominated trust bank, with a required deposit of about P2 million and an additional P500,000 for each consolidator in each country of operation.
Unregistered entities operating as deconsolidators face a P300,000 fine for the first offense and blacklisting for the second.
Forwarders that fail to process, clear or deliver balikbayan boxes to ultimate consignees without a valid justification will face immediate suspension until reactivated by Customs.

As peso weakens, gold prices drop
MANILA, Philippines — The country’s dollar reserves fell further to $97.4 billion in October, weighed down by foreign exchange operations, declining gold prices and government withdrawals amid continued pressure on the peso.
Preliminary data from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) showed gross international reserves (GIR) declined by 2.2 percent from $99.49 billion in September. The latest level was also 11.7 percent lower than the $110.25 billion recorded in October last year.
GIR refers to the central bank’s holdings of foreign assets, including gold, securities and foreign currency deposits, which help finance imports, settle foreign debt and cushion the economy against external shocks.
The BSP attributed the decline to its net foreign exchange operations, downward valuation adjustments primarily involving gold and the national government’s foreign currency withdrawals for debt payments and other funding requirements.
Foreign exchange operations may include buying or selling dollars to smooth sharp fluctuations in the peso. The local currency came under pressure in October, reaching an intraday record low of 64.2 against the dollar on Oct. 27.
UnionBank chief economist Ruben Carlo Asuncion said the reserve decline warrants monitoring, although the country continues to maintain sufficient external buffers.
“The year-on-year decline in reserves is significant and bears watching, but at $97.4 billion, we are not yet looking at a reserve-adequacy problem,” Asuncion said.
“More important than the absolute level is the pace and persistence of the drawdown, particularly if accompanied by sustained peso pressure,” he added.
By component, gold reserves declined by 4.9 percent to $16.95 billion in October from a month ago, while foreign currency securities fell by 1.7 percent to $62.84 billion.
Other reserve assets slipped by 7.5 percent to $9.24 billion, partly offset by higher currency and deposits, which rose to $3.65 billion.
Despite the decline, the BSP said reserves remained an “adequate external liquidity buffer,” equivalent to 6.1 months of imports and payments for services and primary income.
Reserves could also cover 3.1 times the country’s short-term external debt, including loan principal payments falling due within a year.
Asuncion warned that persistent peso weakness could trigger further reserve drawdowns.
“For now, the external buffer remains adequate, but continued reserve losses could gradually reduce the BSP’s room to manage external shocks and excessive forex volatility,” he said.

MANILA, Philippines — The country’s telco providers have piled up almost P18 billion in foreign exchange losses due to the peso’s weakness, adding pressure to efforts to make connectivity affordable.
PLDT Inc., Globe Telecom Inc. and Dito CME Holdings Corp. sustained a combined P17.6 billion in losses because of forex swings in the first half, based on financial reports.
Philippine Chamber of Telecommunication Operators vice president Roy Ibay said the losses are due to telcos paying dollar-based expenses, especially loans.
The losses are adding pressure on telcos to find ways to keep internet prices affordable. However, if they raise prices, they might lose consumers who have also seen their buying power weaken as the peso declined.
PLDT has recognized forex losses of P1.37 billion as of June, from a gain of P1.41 billion a year ago. Globe also endured forex losses of P2.36 billion during the same period.
Of the three, Dito had it worst, suffering forex losses of P13.88 billion because of its exposure to several foreign currency-denominated loans, including the Chinese yuan.
“In the telco industry, forex volatility and currency devaluations heavily impact our expenditures, particularly in emerging markets relying on imported technologies,” Ibay told The STAR.
“(A) telco operator’s revenue is earned in the local currency, but its infrastructure, software and financing are often priced in global currencies like the dollar,” he added.
Ibay cited, for one, the letters of credit to secure network hardware. When the peso dips, the cost to settle these LCs go up, and is reflected as a forex loss for the telco.
Likewise, Ibay said telcos pay dollar-based subscriptions for bandwidth capacity to activate their roaming services abroad, which usually cater to overseas Filipino workers. They are also charged settlement fees for subsea cables used for data transfers among and between countries.
Telcos also import some of the most critical components to keep connectivity running, including radio access networks, fiber lines, base stations and antennas.
“Since components are purchased from global manufacturing giants, local currency depreciation immediately increases procurement costs,” Ibay said.
PLDT senior vice president and enterprise business head Patricio Pineda III said the telco has put in place spending controls to keep expenses in check as the peso declines.
Pineda said PLDT earns part of its revenue in dollars, but is mitigated by the amount of imports it makes to support network expansion. For enterprise, the telco works with foreign suppliers that are paid in dollars.
As such, Pineda hopes the peso recovers to give business and consumers some breathing room. It will also allow telcos to temper costs so they may keep connectivity affordable.
According to a study by Ookla, data costs in the Philippines have declined by two-thirds to P7.07 per GB, from P21.5 per GB in 2023.
The peso last week pulled back to the 63-per-dollar level, recovering after plunging to a record-low 64.17 on Oct. 27, as global oil prices declined following the US midterm elections.
There are indicators the peso may benefit from the overwhelming win of Democratic lawmakers, who are expected to challenge US President Donald Trump’s war on Iran that has triggered the spike in global oil prices.

MANILA, Philippines — Philippine banks may see slower loan growth as weak economic activity dampens borrowing demand and elevated interest rates put pressure on some borrowers, according to the Bankers Association of the Philippines.
BAP president Ana Aboitiz Delgado said lending could moderate as both banks and borrowers turn more cautious amid challenging economic conditions.
“I think loan growth will probably be a little bit slower as you can expect in a slower economy,” Delgado told reporters.
She said the slowdown would reflect not only tighter lending conditions but also subdued demand from businesses and consumers.
“Some of it is deliberate and some of it is just that there’s not a lot of demand right now,” she said.
Bank lending measures credit extended to businesses and households, which supports investment, consumption and broader economic activity.

The Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) recently ruled that a person who departs the US on advance parole could trigger the 3/10-year bar and may not be able to return for a decade. My advice: if you have advance parole (through Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals [DACA] or a pending adjustment of status application), do not travel outside the US. Or first consult with an immigration attorney before doing so.
Advance parole (AP) is permission to leave the US for a brief trip abroad, but more importantly, permission to return to the US after that trip. Many DACA recipients, as well as those with pending adjustment of status applications, would apply for advance parole. This was important, because there is a law that if a person has been out of status for more than 180 days and then departs the US, they could be banned from returning for between three and 10 years.

Civil society this week called on the Philippines to strengthen its economy rather than compromise its sovereignty to appease China and ease tensions in the West Philippine Sea. It asserted that economic strength should enable the country to defend its sovereignty, not become a reason to surrender it. The call comes in response to certain Philippine business groups urging Manila and Beijing to de-escalate tensions amid concerns over trade, investment and employment.
I totally agree. These so-called business groups’ blanket call for de-escalation is an exercise in selective blindness, conveniently glossing over who the aggressor is and the glaring power imbalance between the Philippines and China.
